title: Radical and complex conjugate roots
terms: Conjugate Radical Roots theorem; Complex Conjugate Roots theorem; quadratic conju- gate; real coefficient; rational coefficient.

exposition.text:
For a polynomial with real coefficients, p(z) = p(z). Consequently nonreal roots occur in
complex-conjugate pairs, with equal multiplicities. This need not hold for polynomials with
genuinely complex coefficients. An odd-degree real polynomial therefore has at least one real
root.
√
For rational coefficients, if a + b d is a root with a, b ∈ Q, b ̸= 0, and d ∈ Q nonsquare, then
√
a − b d is also a root. These hypotheses matter: not every irrational number belongs to a
quadratic radical pair. With several independent square roots, more conjugates may be forced;
eliminating the radicals can produce a polynomial and indicate the required degree.

question.text:
√
What is the least possible degree of a nonzero polynomial in Q[x] having both 1 + 2 and 2 + i
as roots?
(A) 2 (B) 3 (C) 4 (D) 5 (E) 6

solution.text:
√
Rational coefficients force 1 − 2, and real coefficients force 2 − i. These four roots are dis-
2 2
tinct, so degree at least 4 is required. The product (x − 2x − 1)(x − 4x + 5) achieves degree
4.

question.text:
A monic real quartic has roots 1 + i and 2 + 3i. What is its constant term?
(A) 52 (B) 25 (C) 26 (D) 20 (E) 13

solution.text:
2 2
The conjugates are also roots. Their product is |1 + i| |2 + 3i| = 2 · 13 = 26, which is the
constant term of a monic quartic.
